entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.50.1">Gen 50:1</reference>-3. <div eID="gen601" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Burial of Jacob.</title> <div sID="gen602" type="x-p"/> When Jacob died, Joseph fell upon the face of his beloved father, wept over him, and kissed him. He then gave the body to the physicians to be embalmed, according to the usual custom in Egypt. The physicians are called his servants, because the reference is to the regular physicians in the service of Joseph, the eminent minister of state; and according to Herod. 2, 84, there were special physicians in Egypt for every description of disease, among whom the <hi type="italic">Taricheuta</hi>, who superintended the embalming, were included, as a special but subordinate class. The process of embalming lasted 40 days, and the solemn mourning 70 (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.3">Gen 50:3</reference>). This is in harmony with the statements of Herodotus and Diodorus when rightly understood (see Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Egypt and the Books of Moses</hi>, p. 67ff.).

The process of embalming lasted 40 days, and the solemn mourning 70 (Gen 50:3). This is in harmony with the statements of Herodotus and Diodorus when rightly understood (see Hengstenberg, Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 67ff.).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.50.4-Gen.50.5">Gen 50:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen603" type="x-p"/> At the end of this period of mourning, Joseph requested “the house of Pharaoh,” i.e., the attendants upon the king, to obtain Pharaoh’s permission for him to go to Canaan and bury his father, according to his last will, in the cave prepared by him there. כּרה (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.5">Gen 50:5</reference>) signifies “to dig” (used, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:14</reference>, for the preparation of a tomb), not “to buy,” In the expression לי כּריתי Jacob attributes to himself as patriarch what had really been done by Abraham (Gen 24). Joseph required the royal permission, because he wished to go beyond the border with his family and a large procession. But he did not apply directly to Pharaoh, because his deep mourning (unshaven and unadorned) prevented him from appearing in the presence of the king.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.50.6-Gen.50.9">Gen 50:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen604" type="x-p"/> After the king’s permission had been obtained, the corpse was carried to Canaan, attended by a large company. With Joseph there went up “<hi type="italic">all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt,</hi>” i.e., the leading officers of the court and state, “<hi type="italic">and all the house of Joseph, and his brethren, and his father’s house,</hi>” i.e., all the members of the families of Joseph, of his brethren, and of is deceased father, “<hi type="italic">excepting only their children and flocks; also chariots and horsemen,</hi>” as an escort for the journey through the desert, “<hi type="italic">a very large army</hi>.” The splendid retinue of Egyptian officers may be explained, in part from the esteem in which Joseph was held in Egypt, and in part from the fondness of the Egyptians for such funeral processions (cf. <hi type="italic">Hengst</hi>. pp. 70, 71).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.50.10-Gen.50.11">Gen 50:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen605" type="x-p"/> Thus they came to <hi type="italic">Goren Atad</hi> beyond the Jordan, as the procession did not take the shortest route by Gaza through the country of the Philistines, probably because so large a procession with a military escort was likely to meet with difficulties there, but went round by the Dead Sea. There, on the border of Canaan, a great mourning and funeral ceremony was kept up for seven days, from which the Canaanites, who watched it from Canaan, gave the place the name of <hi type="italic">Abel-mizraim</hi>, i.e., meadow (אבל with a play upon אבל mourning) of the Egyptians. The situation of <hi type="italic">Goren Atad</hi> (the buck-thorn floor), or <hi type="italic">Abel-mizraim</hi>, has not been discovered. According to <reference osisRef="Gen.50.11">Gen 50:11</reference>, it was on the other side, i.e., the eastern side, of the Jordan. This is put beyond all doubt by <reference osisRef="Gen.50.12">Gen 50:12</reference>, where the sons of Jacob are said to have carried the corpse into the land of Canaan (the land on this side) after the mourning at Goren Atad.<note placement="foot">Consequently the statement of <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Onam. s. v. Area Atad</hi> - “<hi type="italic">locus trans Jordanem, in quo planxerunt quondam Jacob, tertio ab Jerico lapide, duobus millibus ab Jordane, qui nunc vocatur Bethagla, quod interpretatur locus gyri, eo quod ibi more plangentium circumierint in funere Jacob</hi>” - is wrong. <hi type="italic">Beth Agla</hi> cannot be the same as <hi type="italic">Goren Atad</hi>, if only because of the distances given by <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> from Jericho and the Jordan. They do not harmonize at all with his <hi type="italic">trans Jordanem</hi>, which is probably taken from this passage, but point to a place on this side of the Jordan; but still more, because <hi type="italic">Beth Hagla</hi> was on the frontier of Benjamin towards Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.6">Jos 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.18.19">Jos 18:19</reference>), and its name has been retained in the fountain and tower of <hi type="italic">Hajla</hi>, an hour and a quarter to the S.E. of <hi type="italic">Riha</hi> (Jericho), and three-quarters of an hour from the Jordan, by which the site of the ancient <hi type="italic">Beth Hagla</hi> is certainly determined. (Vid., Robinson, <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi>, ii. p. 268ff.)</note>

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.50.15-Gen.50.21">Gen 50:15-21</reference> <div eID="gen607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen608" type="x-p"/> After their father’s death, Joseph’s brethren were filled with alarm, and said, “<hi type="italic">If Joseph now should punish us and requite all the evil that we have done to him,</hi>” sc., what would become of us! The sentence contains an <hi type="italic">aposiopesis</hi>, like <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>; and לוּ with the imperfect presupposes a condition, being used “in cases which are not desired, and for the present not real, though perhaps possible” (<hi type="italic">Ew</hi>. §358). The brethren therefore deputed one of their number (possibly Benjamin) to Joseph, and instructed him to appeal to the wish expressed by their father before his death, and to implore forgiveness: “<hi type="italic">O pardon the misdeed of thy brethren and their sin, that they have done thee evil; and now grant forgiveness to the misdeed of the servants of the God of thy father</hi>.” The ground of their plea is contained in ועתּה “and now,” sc., as we request it by the desire and direction of our father, and in the epithet applied to themselves, “servants of the God of thy father.” There is no reason whatever for regarding the appeal to their father’s wish as a mere pretence. The fact that no reference was made by Jacob in his blessing to their sin against Joseph, merely proved that he as their father had forgiven the sin of his sons, since the grace of God had made their misdeed the means of Israel’s salvation; but it by no means proves that he could not have instructed his sons humbly to beg for forgiveness from Joseph, even though Joseph had hitherto shown them only goodness and love. How far Joseph was from thinking of ultimate retribution and revenge, is evident from the reception which he gave to their request (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.17">Gen 50:17</reference>): “<hi type="italic">Joseph wept at their address to him</hi>.” viz., at the fact that they could impute anything so bad to him; and when they came themselves, and threw themselves as servants at his feet, he said to them (<reference osisRef="Gen.50.19">Gen 50:19</reference>), “<hi type="italic">Fear not, for am I in the place of God?</hi>” i.e., am I in a position to interfere of my own accord with the purposes of God, and not rather bound to submit to them myself? “<hi type="italic">Ye had indeed evil against me in your mind, but God had it in mind for good </hi>(to turn this evil into good), <hi type="italic">to do</hi> (עשׂה like ואה <reference osisRef="Gen.48.11">Gen 48:11</reference>), <hi type="italic">as is now evident</hi> (lit., as has occurred this day, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.2.30">Deu 2:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">Deu 4:20</reference>, etc.), <hi type="italic">to preserve alive a great nation</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.45.7">Gen 45:7</reference>). <hi type="italic">And now fear not, I shall provide for you and your families</hi>.” Thus he quieted them by his affectionate words.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Gen.50.22-Gen.50.23">Gen 50:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen609" type="x-p"/> Death of Joseph. - Joseph lived to see the commencement of the fulfilment of his father’s blessing. Having reached the age of 110, he saw Ephraim’s שׁלּשׁים בּני “<hi type="italic">sons of the third link,</hi>” i.e., of great-grandsons, consequently great-great-grandsons. שׁלּשׁים descendants in the third generation are expressly distinguished from “children’s children” or grandsons in Exo 34:7. There is no practical difficulty in the way of this explanation, the only one which the language will allow. As Joseph’s two sons were born before he was 37 years old (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.50">Gen 41:50</reference>), and Ephraim therefore was born, at the latest, in his 36th year, and possibly in his 34th, since Joseph was married in his 31st year, he might have had grandsons by the time he was 56 or 60 years old, and great-grandsons when he was from 78 to 85, so that great-great-grandsons might have been born when he was 100 or 110 years old. To regard the “sons of the third generation” as children in the third generation (great-grandsons of Joseph and grandsons of Ephraim), as many commentators do, as though the construct בּני stood for the absolute, is evidently opposed to the context, since it is stated immediately afterwards, that sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, i.e., great-grandsons, were also born upon his knees, i.e., so that he could take them also upon his knees and show them his paternal love. There is no reason for thinking of adoption in connection with these words. And if Joseph lived to see only the great-grandsons of Ephraim as well as of Manasseh, it is difficult to imagine why the same expression should not be applied to the grandchildren of Manasseh, as to the descendants of Ephraim.

entries.content_osis:
Gen 50:24-26
When Joseph saw his death approaching, he expressed to his brethren his firm belief in the fulfilment of the divine promise (Gen 46:4-5, cf. Gen 15:16, Gen 15:18.), and made them take an oath, that if God should bring them into the promised land, they would carry his bones with them from Egypt. This last desire of his was carried out.
